content.thinking:
I'm lining up the timeline: onset occurred right around the P2 deploy, while the earlier P1 change happened four hours prior, which likely rules it out as the cause. I also note the flag provider logs show zero recent flag changes, further narrowing the culprit toward the deploy itself.

I'm checking for a discrepancy between the diff, which directly shows record_purchase being modified, versus an unverified claim about a derived function name — I should treat that claim cautiously since it isn't confirmed by the record. Piecing together the likely root cause: the change appears to have stopped updating the stored month total while readers continue to report that stale stored figure, which matches the alert's full failure count and explains why totals aren't reconciling.

For the timeline, I'm factoring in the detection gap from the periodic check interval, meaning the fault could have gone unnoticed for several days before being caught, along with contributing factors like the lack of a reconciliation test and no automatic rollback since nothing existed to verify one. For action items beyond the merge fix and rollback, I'm considering proposing a manual repair script run, more frequent reconciliation checks, a CI test asserting stored totals match actual purchases, and a process requiring readers to migrate before any stored field gets dropped.

I want to keep all figures as variables rather than literal numbers, using placeholders like durations and counts instead of digits, while still allowing labels like action item numbers to stay as-is since they're identifiers, not data points.

I'm also ruling out one provider's change as the cause since the onset timing follows the other provider's change instead, with no flag modifications showing up in that first provider's record — I need to state this carefully without overclaiming what the diff actually shows. Then I start laying out the first step of the symptom chain, where shopper totals were short by a certain amount across the full set.

The actual root cause becomes clear: the release stopped writing the stored month total under the assumption it could be derived from history instead, but something was still reading that stale stored figure, so it silently drifted with every new purchase and nothing paged since the service kept running fast with no errors. I'm drafting the remediation plan now — a repair script, a deploy-time check, a CI reconciliation test, and a process change to migrate how totals are read.

I should also note that rollback alone won't fix already-corrupted records, so that needs calling out in the went-wrong section, while crediting that Argus caught the deployment quickly and wisely avoided an automatic rollback. The open assumptions worth flagging: unverified error rates, unread logs, and the static F1 reading that hasn't been independently confirmed.

Now I'll write the executive summary without naming specific components.

action_items.item: After the fix is deployed, run scripts/repair_monthly_totals.py against the production account records. Run it first without --apply and check that it finds the {A1} short accounts, then with --apply, then load the output back into the store. Do not run it before the fix is live or new purchases will drift again. Review the list of accounts whose totals are too high separately.
Run the month-total reconciliation check on every deploy and on a schedule much shorter than {A5} days, and page on the first mismatch.
Add a test, run before release, that records purchases through every write path, both in and out of the current month, and asserts that the stored month total equals the sum of the month's purchases.
Before a stored figure is removed or no longer maintained, require that every reader is first moved to a derived value. Add this as a review checklist item for ledger changes.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' stored totals did not match the purchases behind them: {A1} of {A2} were short, the widest by {A3}, and the oldest affected purchase was recorded at {A4}. Nothing errored or slowed. The metrics read had no calm hour before the onset, so no error-rate rise could be measured, and no logs were read.

The stored month total was not being increased when purchases were recorded after the onset, so each one left it further behind the history. The onset, {began}, comes {began - P2.1} after the second production change.

The deployment of 26f1d7e removed the month-total update from record_purchase. The diff drops the line that added a purchase to total_this_month_cents, and the new docstring says the month 'is no longer carried' and can be worked out from the history on demand. Only the lifetime total is still added to.

The stored figure was still the one being read, and nothing derived the month from the purchases in its place. This rests only on a static reading of the code that nothing ran, so it is unverified: it says the average-spend function and the monthly statement still read the stored month total. If so, every purchase recorded since the deploy widened the gap with no error, which fits {A1} of {A2} accounts being short and flat metrics.

Other candidates the record does not support. The earlier deploy 4c810f2 came {began - P1.1} before the onset, not at it, and the diff read shows the removal in 26f1d7e. The flag provider showed {T13.2} recent flag changes, so a flag flip does not explain the start. The record does not show why the release dropped the stored total before its readers were moved over.

contributing_factors.factor: The only check that caught the fault was the spend-integrity check, which runs every {A5} days. The fault therefore ran undetected for up to that long and the damage grew meanwhile. No faster reconciliation check was seen in the record.

No test or pre-release check was seen that would fail when a write path leaves the stored month total out of step with the purchases. The change that stopped maintaining it went to production without one.

Rolling back was not taken automatically. Argus judged it sound but found nothing would show inside its waiting time whether it worked, so it was left for a person. A rollback also does not repair totals already written wrong.
The change dropped a stored figure while code that reads it appears (unverified, static reading) to have been left unchanged. No review step was seen that checks the readers of a removed field.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers' month-to-date spend totals were silently wrong. A release changed the shop so that it stopped keeping that total up to date when a purchase was recorded. Every purchase after the release left the stored total further behind. By the time a weekly integrity check caught it, {A1} of {A2} shopper totals no longer matched their purchases, and the widest was short by {A3}. The service stayed fast and raised no errors, so nothing paged. The incident was open for at least {duration}, and that is a lower bound. Argus tied the start to the release, recommended a rollback and left it for a person to carry out. A draft fix and a one-off repair script were proposed, but neither had been applied or run when the incident was closed. Totals already written stay wrong until they are repaired.

got_lucky: The purchase history itself appears to be intact, since the repair script rebuilds the month total from it. That comes from a static reading and was not run. The damage looks limited to the derived total, which is recoverable, not the purchases.
went_well: Argus tied the start of the incident to the deployment and read what it changed within seconds of the alert.
The diff and the flag history were both checked, so a flag change was shown not to be the trigger.
A draft fix and a repair script that reports before it writes were produced soon after the investigation.
went_wrong: The fault ran for at least {duration} before the alert, found by a periodic check rather than by a live signal.
Error and latency metrics stayed flat, so the usual signals could not show this fault.
The rollback and the fix were still open when the incident was closed, and the repair had not been run, so the wrong totals remained.

input.root_cause: A release changed how a purchase is recorded so that the stored month total on a shopper's account is no longer updated, on the idea that the month can be worked out from the purchase history. The stored figure is still the one reported, so it fell further behind with every purchase and raised no error. The last link is unverified: that readers still use the stored figure comes from a static reading of the code that nothing ran.
input.symptom: Shoppers' month-to-date spend totals were too low
